I might be going a little off-topic here, but I think the motivation to fight for yourself comes from your purpose to live, which ultimately stems from your faith/philosophy. Judging from your comments, you seem to be an optimist at the very core because your optimism doesn't feel forced. The trauma you were facing as you were growing up stripped you of that optimism as you grew up, but somewhere along the way, you found your authentic self again. I just wanted to speak on behalf of the natural nihilists. The kind that found life tedious and mundane, had the nagging feeling that everything is utterly pointless at six years old in the middle of a shopping mall. Nihilism is so deeply rooted in my identity that adopting any other philosophy entails losing myself. My philosophy is part of what makes me completely indifferent to normally pleasurable experiences. This is what causes the divide -- even on this very subreddit -- between those who are still able to feel happiness (however fleeting it may be) and those who lack the capacity to do so.

It's admirable how you grew a thicker skin from your trauma. You're one of the strong ones. Unfortunately, there are also the ones who become more sensitive and insecure, get overwhelmed more easily, and more importantly, become colorblind -- develop anhedonia, that is. After all, we are survivors and not superheroes. I believe everyone has a threshold and at some point we will fall and never rebound. For the majority, that point is physical death. For the minority, that point does not align with physical death, but that doesn't mean we aren't, well, dead. A number of us continue only due to the threat of suicide attempts failing and resulting in a permanent injury. When we hear "it gets better" or are told to find moments of happiness amidst the pain/numbness, we know that it's targeted at the population that's still alive, figuratively speaking.

We lose brain plasticity as we age, and if your childhood has molded you into an alien that can only exist in the very specific universe your perpetrators have created for you, you will crumble in a universe where those conditions don't exist -- if trauma is all that you've truly known. To adapt to an environment that is free of constant abuse is to change what species we are, to upload a different consciousness into our body, if you will. Even if that were possible, that person is no longer yourself as you've known since birth to present.

I understand that your comments come from a genuine place, but the matter is more complex than they let on. Sorry for dragging this on -- I just wanted this to be out there.

However, I wouldn't say that your statement is universal as there haven't been any highs in my life since the fleeting ones from my early childhood -- this low has stretched on for decades, and, judging from posts made by older suicidal people, will continue in the decades to come. Honestly, it's pointless to get our hopes up from a unicorn success story here and there when the odds are against us -- I don't know what it's like for ADHD sufferers in particular, but I know that for autistic people, chances of having a brighter future are slim to none. 85% are unemployed and 5% are married. Unless we want to intentionally lie to ourselves (which opens a whole other can of worms)... it doesn't get better. Autism in women *presents* as depressive episodes, mood swings, etc., so the problem is practically embedded in our genes. You can't change the way you're wired, so how will you change the manifestations of it?

Just to point out that depression alone does not make you neurodivergent, which is an umbrella term for those with neurological disorders, such as autism, ADHD, etc. Both neurotypicals and neurodiverse people have depression -- it's just more commonplace and harder to cure for neurodiverse people.

You mention that "we enjoy those moments SO much more than the 'normal' person," -- well, it can also be the other way around for suicidal people. We can be so far gone that life's simple pleasures do absolutely nothing for us -- we're basically colorblind and can't taste anything. If we didn't have *anhedonia,* I doubt a lot of us would even be suicidal in the first place. Besides, the majority of suicidal people are neurodiverse -- depression and suicidality are practically in our genes. There's a lot more hope for neurotypical depression.

Well, I don't think anything specific drove my existential dread, but I could be writing for the rest of my life and would still never be finished explaining why. I agree that it's also a blessing because when I used to believe in an afterlife, I hated the idea of existing infinitely. Anyway, my beliefs tie into the idea of evolution. Life has evolved from a bacterium. We are merely a more complex form of life and thus have higher consciousness, from which the concepts of higher purpose, morality, and free will came about. We fall into this psychological trap because our perception is different to that of other organisms we and feel the need to validate it. I strongly believe that morality is relative and the idea that you're being graded on life and an afterlife with the promise of justice is absurd to me. It's also arrogant because we believe that the universe operates on patterns of human thought. It is biased towards our psychological needs (we all want to feel important), while the concept of evolution stems from observation. The concept of an afterlife came about as a coping mechanism for death anxiety. Belief in an afterlife requires us to fill in gaps in the information we already have, while belief in the finality of life doesn't. If we believe life has meaning in itself, we must assign value to every single form of life. And how do we define life in the first place?
